sets.passage:
Magnetic navigation in birds

Every autumn, many songbirds fly thousands of kilometers to warmer regions, often at night and over unfamiliar land. For decades, scientists wondered how such small animals could hold a course with so few visible landmarks. One important answer appears to be the Earth's magnetic field.

In laboratory studies, researchers placed migrating birds in round cages surrounded by electric coils. When the coils were switched on, they shifted the direction of the magnetic field. The birds responded by hopping toward a new side of the cage, as if they were trying to fly in a different direction. This suggested that the birds were sensing magnetic north.

How they sense it is still debated. One theory points to special proteins in the eye that react to magnetism when struck by light. If this is correct, birds might literally see the magnetic field as a faint pattern across their view. Notably, the birds' magnetic sense seems to work poorly in complete darkness, which supports this idea. Most researchers now believe that birds combine this sense with the positions of the stars and the sun.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why songbirds migrate at night rather than during the day
How migrating birds may use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way
Why birds become confused by unfamiliar landmarks
How electric coils are used to protect birds during migration
questions.why: 第1段落末で答え（地磁気）を出し、実験と仕組みの説で展開している。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what did the birds do when the coils were switched on?
choices: They tried to escape from the top of the cage.
They stopped moving completely.
They moved toward a different part of the cage.
They began to sing more loudly.
questions.why: 第2段落：hopping toward a new side of the cage。

questions.q: The word "faint" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: weak
moving
colorful
sharp
questions.why: faint pattern＝かすかな模様。weak が最も近い。

questions.q: Why does the author mention that the magnetic sense works poorly in complete darkness?
choices: To show that birds cannot migrate at night
To argue that stars are more important than magnetism
To explain why the laboratory studies failed
To support the idea that light is involved in sensing magnetism
questions.why: 光で反応するタンパク質説の直後に which supports this idea とある。

questions.q: What can be inferred about bird navigation from the final sentence?
choices: The magnetic sense is useless without the sun.

Scientists have stopped studying the magnetic sense.
Stars are visible to birds only in autumn.
questions.why: combine this sense with the stars and the sun＝複数の手がかりを使う。

sets.passage:
Reading rock layers

Cliffs and canyon walls often show bands of rock stacked on top of one another. These layers, called strata, form when sediment such as sand, mud, or shells settles in water and is slowly pressed into stone. Because new sediment is laid down on top of older material, geologists generally assume that lower layers are older than the ones above them. This simple rule allows them to place events in order even without knowing exact dates.

The record is rarely perfect, however. In some places, a layer is missing because rivers or wind removed it before the next layer formed. These gaps, known as unconformities, can represent millions of years. In mountain regions, powerful forces in the crust may even fold rock layers so sharply that older strata end up above younger ones.

To deal with such problems, geologists compare layers across wide areas. A distinctive layer, such as one containing a particular fossil or a thin band of volcanic ash, can serve as a marker. If the same marker appears in two distant cliffs, the rocks around it are probably of similar age.

questions.q: According to the passage, why are lower strata usually older?
choices: Newer sediment settles on top of older sediment.
Older rock is heavier and sinks.
Lower layers contain more shells.
Water pressure is greater near the bottom.
questions.why: 第1段落：new sediment is laid down on top of older material。

questions.q: The word "distinctive" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: extremely thin
commonly found
very old
easy to recognize
questions.why: distinctive＝はっきり区別できる。marker として使えるのは見分けやすいから。

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a reason the rock record can be incomplete or confusing?
choices: Rivers removing a layer

Researchers have also found small white lumps of lime scattered throughout Roman concrete. These were once dismissed as a sign of careless mixing. More recent studies, however, suggest that the lumps were useful: when water entered a crack, it dissolved some of the lime, which then hardened again and sealed the gap. People generally want their beliefs and actions to fit together. When they notice a conflict between the two, they often feel uncomfortable. Psychologists call this feeling cognitive dissonance, and they have found that people work hard to reduce it.

In a well-known type of experiment, participants complete a boring task and are then asked to tell the next participant that it was enjoyable. Some are paid a large amount for saying this, while others receive only a small amount. Later, when asked how much they actually liked the task, those who were paid very little tend to rate it more positively. The researchers' explanation is that well-paid participants could justify their statement by the money. Poorly paid participants had no such excuse, so they reduced their discomfort by changing their opinion of the task.

Dissonance can affect many everyday decisions. After buying an expensive product, for example, shoppers often pay more attention to positive reviews and ignore negative ones. By focusing on information that supports their choice, they protect themselves from the feeling that they may have made a mistake.

Other factors add to the problem. Cities have fewer trees and less open soil, so less water evaporates to cool the air. Tall buildings can block wind that would otherwise carry heat away. Cars, air conditioners, and factories also give off heat directly.

The effect is more than a matter of comfort. Higher night temperatures can make heat waves more dangerous, especially for older people, and they increase the demand for electricity. As a result, many cities are experimenting with solutions. Painting roofs white or light gray reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it. Planting street trees provides shade, and parks with grass and ponds help cool nearby neighborhoods. Some cities have even replaced parking lots with surfaces that allow rainwater to soak into the ground.

For a long time, scientists assumed that almost all life on Earth depended on energy from the sun. Plants capture sunlight, and animals eat plants or other animals. That assumption was challenged when explorers discovered communities of animals living around hot springs on the dark ocean floor.

These hot springs, called hydrothermal vents, release water heated by volcanic activity beneath the seabed. The water is rich in dissolved chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide, which is poisonous to most animals. Yet certain bacteria can use these chemicals to make food, a process called chemosynthesis. The bacteria form the base of a food web that includes giant tube worms, clams, shrimp, and crabs.

Some vent animals have formed remarkable partnerships with the bacteria. Adult giant tube worms have no mouth or stomach. Instead, they carry bacteria inside their bodies and supply them with chemicals from the water, and the bacteria in turn provide the worms with nutrients. Discoveries like these have encouraged scientists to consider whether life might exist in similar dark environments elsewhere, such as the oceans thought to lie beneath the ice of some moons.

Perspective in Renaissance painting

Before the fifteenth century, many European paintings showed figures and buildings in a way that looked flat. Important people were often painted larger than others, regardless of where they stood in the scene. During the Renaissance, however, artists in Italy developed a system called linear perspective that made flat surfaces appear to have depth.

The key idea of linear perspective is the vanishing point. Lines that are parallel in real life, such as the edges of a road or the rows of tiles on a floor, are drawn so that they meet at a single point on the horizon. Objects are also made smaller as they move farther from the viewer. Together, these rules create a convincing sense of distance.

The new method spread quickly, partly because it was closely linked to mathematics and could be taught step by step. Artists' guidebooks explained how to construct a scene with rulers and measured lines. Perspective changed not only painting but also architecture and stage design, and it remained the standard way of representing space in Western art for several centuries.

Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time. Clocks were set so that noon was the moment the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the sun reaches that point at slightly different moments in different places, a town to the east would be a few minutes ahead of a town to the west.

These small differences caused few problems when travel was slow. The spread of railways changed that. A train might pass through dozens of towns, each with its own time, and printed timetables became extremely confusing. Some stations displayed several clocks at once, one for each railway company that used them.

To solve the problem, railway companies began to adopt standard time, in which every place within a large region used the same clock time. The idea met some resistance at first, as people were used to following the sun. Over time, however, governments made standard time official, and the world was eventually divided into time zones. Traditional economic theory assumes that people make choices by carefully weighing costs and benefits. Behavioral economists, however, have shown that the way choices are presented can strongly influence what people decide, even when the options themselves stay the same.

One powerful example is the default option, which is what happens if a person does nothing. In many workplaces, employees can join a retirement savings plan. When joining requires filling out a form, a large share of workers never sign up. When workers are enrolled automatically and must fill out a form to leave, participation often rises sharply. The plan and its benefits are identical in both cases; only the default has changed.

Several explanations have been offered. Making a decision takes effort, and people tend to put off tasks that are not urgent. Some may also see the default as a recommendation from the employer. Supporters argue that well-designed defaults can help people act in their own long-term interest. Critics reply that defaults may push people toward choices they would not make on reflection, so they should be used openly and with care.

Octopuses are famous for changing color in less than a second. Unlike most animals, which change color slowly through hormones, octopuses control their skin directly with their nervous system. Their skin contains thousands of small sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each surrounded by tiny muscles. When the muscles pull, a sac stretches open and its color spreads; when they relax, the sac shrinks to a dot.

This ability serves several purposes. Most obviously, it helps octopuses hide from predators by matching the rocks or sand around them. Some species can also change the texture of their skin, raising small bumps that make them resemble seaweed. Color change is used for communication as well. Males of some species display bold stripes when competing for mates, while others flash dark colors to warn rivals away.

One puzzle has long interested researchers. Most octopuses appear to be color-blind, yet they match their surroundings remarkably well. Some scientists suggest that light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself might allow the animals to detect color without using their eyes. This idea has not yet been confirmed, but it would help explain their impressive skill.

Researchers are careful to note the limits of this effect. Placebos may change how people feel, but they rarely change the underlying condition, such as a broken bone or high blood sugar. Instead, some researchers are studying how the expectations that create the placebo effect might be used to make real treatments work better.

Elsewhere, deep water gradually rises back to the surface to replace it, completing a loop that can take around a thousand years.

This slow loop matters for both life and climate. Rising deep water brings nutrients up from the bottom, supporting large populations of fish. The circulation also moves heat from warm regions toward cold ones. Some scientists are concerned that melting ice could add fresh water near the poles, reducing the density of surface water there and weakening the circulation.

choices: Creating strong winds near the poles
Bringing nutrients toward the surface
Supporting large fish populations
Moving heat toward cold regions
questions.why: 栄養・魚・熱の移動は書かれている。風は出てこない。

questions.q: What can be inferred about adding fresh water near the poles?
choices: It would make the loop much faster.
It would make surface water less likely to sink.
It would make the ocean saltier.
It would bring more nutrients to the surface.
questions.why: 真水で密度が下がる→重くならず沈みにくい→循環が弱まる。

sets.passage:
Mangrove forests

Mangroves are trees that grow along tropical coasts, where their roots are covered by seawater at high tide. Few plants can survive in such conditions. Salt water would kill most trees, and the muddy ground contains very little oxygen.

Mangroves have developed several solutions to these problems. Some species block most of the salt at their roots, while others take in salt and push it out through special glands in their leaves. To deal with the lack of oxygen, many mangroves send up thin roots that stick out of the mud like pencils. These roots take in air at low tide and carry it to the parts of the tree buried below.

Mangrove forests are valuable far beyond their own borders. Their tangled roots slow down waves and hold mud in place, protecting the shore from erosion. The calm water between the roots also serves as a nursery for young fish, many of which later move to coral reefs or the open sea. Because of these benefits, many coastal communities now work to protect and replant mangroves.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what makes mangrove habitats difficult for most plants?
choices: Strong winds and cold temperatures
A lack of sunlight under the trees
Salt water and mud with little oxygen
Frequent visits by young fish
questions.why: Salt water would kill most trees, and the muddy ground contains very little oxygen。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how do some mangroves get rid of salt?
choices: By storing it in their thin roots
By releasing it into the air at low tide
By growing only in fresh water
By pushing it out through their leaves
questions.why: push it out through special glands in their leaves。

questions.q: The word "tangled" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: twisted together
very deep
recently grown
easily broken
questions.why: tangled roots＝からみ合った根。

questions.q: Why does the author compare some roots to pencils?
choices: To show that they are used by people for writing
To describe their thin shape as they stick up out of the mud
To explain how they block salt
To suggest that they break easily
questions.why: thin roots that stick out of the mud like pencils＝形のたとえ。

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about coral reefs?
choices: They protect mangroves from waves.
They are being replanted by coastal communities.
Some of their fish may have spent their early lives among mangroves.
They contain no young fish.
questions.why: マングローブで育った若い魚の多くが後でサンゴ礁へ移る。

sets.passage:
Medieval craft guilds

In many medieval European towns, people who practiced the same craft, such as weaving or baking, formed associations called guilds. A guild set rules for its members, including the prices they could charge and the quality their goods had to meet. Often, only guild members were allowed to sell certain products in the town.

Guilds also controlled who could enter a trade. A young person usually began as an apprentice, living with a master and learning the craft for several years, often without pay. Next came a period as a journeyman, a skilled worker paid by the day. To become a master, a journeyman often had to produce a piece of excellent work, which gave us the word "masterpiece."

Historians disagree about the effects of guilds. Some argue that they protected customers by keeping quality high and gave workers security. Others point out that by limiting competition, guilds kept prices high and made it hard for newcomers and new methods to succeed. Both views may be partly true, since guilds varied widely from town to town and changed over time.

questions.q: What is paragraph 2 mainly about?
choices: How guilds set the prices of goods
Why apprentices were paid by the day
How historians judge the value of guilds
The stages a person went through to become a master
questions.why: apprentice → journeyman → master の段階を説明している。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what was a journeyman?
choices: A skilled worker who received daily pay
A young learner who lived with a master
A guild leader who set prices
A trader who traveled between towns
questions.why: a journeyman, a skilled worker paid by the day。

questions.q: Why does the author mention the word "masterpiece"?
choices: To give an example of a product sold only by guilds
To show a connection between a guild custom and a modern word
To explain why apprentices were not paid
To argue that guild work was of low quality
questions.why: 親方になるための優れた作品→masterpiece という語の由来。

questions.q: The word "varied" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: grew
failed
differed
agreed
questions.why: varied widely from town to town＝町ごとに大きく違った。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a possible effect of guilds?
choices: Keeping quality high
Giving workers security
Making it hard for newcomers
Lowering prices for customers
questions.why: 批判側は「価格を高く保った」と言う。安くしたとは書かれていない。

sets.passage:
A critical period for language

Young children seem to learn languages with remarkable ease. Many researchers believe there is a critical period, a window early in life during which the brain is especially ready to acquire language. According to this view, learning becomes harder once the window closes, possibly around the early teenage years.

Evidence comes partly from studies of immigrants. People who moved to a new country as young children usually came to speak the new language without a trace of a foreign accent. Those who arrived as adults often learned vocabulary and grammar well but kept an accent for life. Pronunciation, in particular, appears to depend strongly on the age at which learning begins.

However, the picture is not simple. Adults often learn faster than children at first, because they can use study strategies and understand grammar explanations. Children's advantage seems to appear mainly over the long term and depends on years of rich exposure. Moreover, some adult learners do reach native-like levels, which suggests that the window may narrow gradually rather than close suddenly.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: The idea that age affects how well people learn languages
How immigrants choose a new country
Why adults prefer studying grammar
How young children learn to read
questions.why: critical period（言語を身につけやすい時期）の説と、その証拠・反論。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what was usually true of people who arrived as adults?
choices: They could not learn grammar.
They kept a foreign accent.
They learned faster than children in every area.
They lost their first language.
questions.why: kept an accent for life。文法や語彙はよく覚えた。

questions.q: The word "trace" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: fear
rule
sign
need
questions.why: without a trace of a foreign accent＝外国なまりの跡（しるし）もなく。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, why do adults often learn faster at first?
choices: Their brains are in the critical period.
They receive more exposure than children.
They already have native-like pronunciation.
They can use strategies and understand explanations.
questions.why: because they can use study strategies and understand grammar explanations。

questions.q: What does the author suggest in the last sentence about the critical period?
choices: It may end slowly rather than all at once.
It does not exist at all.
It closes suddenly at age twelve.
It applies only to grammar.
questions.why: the window may narrow gradually rather than close suddenly。

sets.passage:
Tree rings

If you look at the cut surface of a tree trunk, you will usually see a pattern of rings. In regions with distinct seasons, a tree adds one ring each year. Wood formed in spring grows quickly and is light in color, while wood formed later in the year is denser and darker. Counting the rings therefore reveals the tree's age.

The rings record more than age. In a year with plenty of rain and a long growing season, a tree produces a wide ring; in a dry or cold year, the ring is narrow. Because all the trees in an area experience the same weather, they share the same sequence of wide and narrow rings. Scientists can match this pattern across living trees, old buildings, and buried wood to build records that reach back thousands of years.

These records have practical uses. Archaeologists use them to find the year in which wooden beams were cut, which helps date old structures. Climate researchers use ring widths to estimate rainfall in periods before weather instruments existed.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why does wood formed in spring look lighter?
choices: It contains more water.
It grows quickly.
It forms in cold weather.
It is denser than later wood.
questions.why: Wood formed in spring grows quickly and is light in color。濃いのは後の時期の木。

questions.q: The word "distinct" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: very long
unusually warm
clearly different
slowly changing
questions.why: distinct seasons＝はっきり分かれた季節。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what usually causes a narrow ring?
choices: A long growing season
Heavy rain in spring
The great age of a tree
A dry or cold year
questions.why: in a dry or cold year, the ring is narrow。

questions.q: Why does the author mention old buildings and buried wood?
choices: To show where scientists find wood to extend tree-ring records
To explain why some trees grow narrow rings
To argue that old buildings should be protected
To describe how wooden beams are cut
questions.why: 生きている木から古い建物・埋もれた木へ模様をつなぎ、何千年も前までの記録を作る。

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 3?
choices: Weather instruments are less accurate than tree rings.
Tree rings can give information about times before weather records were kept.
Archaeologists no longer need other dating methods.
All old buildings were made from the same trees.
questions.why: before weather instruments existed の時代の雨量を推定できる。

sets.passage:
Network effects

For most products, the value to a buyer does not depend on how many other people own the same thing. A good umbrella keeps you just as dry whether or not your neighbors have one. Some products are different. A telephone is useless if no one else has one, and it becomes more valuable as more people join the network. Economists call this a network effect.

Network effects can lead to rapid growth once a product becomes popular. Each new user makes the product more attractive to the next person, which brings in still more users. For this reason, companies offering such products often sell them cheaply or even give them away at first, hoping to reach a large number of users before their competitors do.

The same process can make markets hard to enter. A new product may be technically better, but if most people already use an older one, few will switch, since much of the value lies in the shared network. As a result, a market with strong network effects may end up dominated by one or two products that were not necessarily the best.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How telephones changed communication
Why companies should always sell products cheaply
How the value of some products grows with the number of users, and what follows from this
How economists measure product quality
questions.why: network effect の定義→急成長→市場に入りにくい、の流れ。

questions.q: Why does the author mention an umbrella?
choices: To show that some products lose value over time
To explain why telephones were invented
To argue that cheap products are popular
To give an example of a product without a network effect
questions.why: 傘は隣人が持っていてもいなくても価値が同じ＝ネットワーク効果の無い例。

questions.q: The word "attractive" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: appealing
expensive
complicated
familiar
questions.why: more attractive to the next person＝次の人にとってより魅力的。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why do some companies give their products away at first?
choices: To test whether the product works
To gain many users before rival companies do
To reduce the cost of the network
To follow government rules
questions.why: hoping to reach a large number of users before their competitors do。

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 3?
choices: New products always replace older ones quickly.
Customers always choose technically better products.
The most popular product in such a market may not be the highest in quality.
Markets with network effects have many equal competitors.
questions.why: not necessarily the best＝一番良い物が勝つとは限らない。

sets.passage:
Ant trails

Anyone who has seen a line of ants marching toward a piece of food may wonder how they organize themselves without a leader. The answer lies largely in chemical signals called pheromones. When a worker ant finds food, it returns to the nest while leaving a trail of pheromone on the ground.

Other ants follow this trail to the food, and as they return, they add pheromone of their own. A short route is traveled more quickly, so it receives more pheromone in a given time, attracting even more ants. Meanwhile, the chemical slowly evaporates, so trails to longer routes or exhausted food sources gradually fade. Without any single ant planning it, the colony tends to settle on the shortest path.

This kind of group behavior, in which simple rules followed by individuals produce intelligent results, is known as collective intelligence. Engineers have borrowed the idea to design computer programs that find efficient routes, for example for delivery trucks. These programs send out many simple "virtual ants" and let the best solutions emerge.

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, what does a worker ant do after finding food?
choices: It carries all the food home at once.
It signals the colony with sound.
It waits beside the food for other ants.
It leaves a chemical trail on its way back to the nest.
questions.why: it returns to the nest while leaving a trail of pheromone。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why does a short route receive more pheromone?
choices: Ants travel it more quickly, so it is used more often in the same time.
Ants leave stronger chemicals on short routes.
The chemical lasts longer on short routes.
A leader ant marks the shortest path.
questions.why: A short route is traveled more quickly, so it receives more pheromone in a given time。

questions.q: The word "exhausted" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: very tired
used up
far away
newly found
questions.why: exhausted food sources＝食べ物が無くなった所。ここでは「疲れた」ではない。

questions.q: What can be inferred about a trail to food that has run out?
choices: It becomes stronger as ants search harder.
It is removed by a leader ant.
Fewer and fewer ants will follow it.
It leads ants to new food sources.
questions.why: 使われない道はフェロモンが蒸発して消えていく。

questions.q: What is the purpose of paragraph 3?
choices: To describe how ants choose a leader
To argue that ants are smarter than computers
To explain why delivery trucks follow ants
To show how the ants' method has been applied in another field
questions.why: アリのやり方を配送ルートのプログラムに応用した例。

parts.title: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response
parts.desc: 1文を聞いて、一番自然な返事を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: 最初の1〜2語（疑問詞・Do/Can/Would）で、何を求められているかを決める。同じ語や似た音をくり返す選択肢はひっかけのことが多い。質問でない文には、提案や気づかいで返すのが自然。
parts.intro: You will hear a person speak. Choose the best response.

sets.script: Do you know when the library closes tonight?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: No, I haven't read it yet.
Yes, I closed it last night.
The library has three floors.
I think it's open until eleven.
questions.why: 閉館時間を聞かれているので時刻で答える。closed / read は音や連想のひっかけ。

sets.script: Would you mind lending me your notes from Monday's lecture?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Yes, I lent it to the professor.
I don't mind the noise.
Sure, I'll send you a copy tonight.
The lecture starts on Monday.
questions.why: Would you mind …? への承諾。Sure, … が自然。

sets.script: Why wasn't Professor Lee in class today?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: She teaches biology and chemistry.
Apparently she's at a conference this week.
Because the class starts at ten.
Yes, she was very clear today.
questions.why: Why の理由に答えている。Yes/No では答えない。

sets.script: I can't find my student ID anywhere.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Did you check the pocket of your jacket?
Yes, it's anywhere you like.
I found the student center.
Your ID number is very long.
questions.why: なくした相手に探す場所を提案するのが自然な返事。

sets.script: Is it too late to drop the statistics course?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Statistics is a difficult subject.
Yes, it was dropped on the floor.
You have until Friday to do it.
I'm usually late on Fridays.
questions.why: 履修の取り消し期限を伝えている。drop の別の意味のひっかけに注意。

sets.script: Have you started the group presentation yet?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Not yet, we're meeting tomorrow to plan it.
The group is very large.
Yes, the present was wrapped.
I'll start the car.
questions.why: まだ／もう始めたか、に答え、予定も添えている。

sets.script: The printer on the second floor is out of paper again.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: I'm out of the office.
It printed in color.
The second floor is quieter.
I'll let the front desk know.
questions.why: 問題の報告に対して、対応を申し出る返事。

sets.script: Which bus goes to the science building?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Science is my favorite subject.
Take the number 4; it stops right in front.
The bus was very crowded.
It goes every day except Sunday.
questions.why: Which bus に対して具体的なバスを答える。

sets.script: Could you remind me what the homework was?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: We have to read chapter six and answer the questions.
Homework is due in the mailbox.
It was a nice reminder.
I'll remind you of my name.
questions.why: 宿題の内容をたずねられている。

sets.script: I'm thinking of joining the photography club.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The club meets on the photo.
I took the picture yesterday.
The photos are on the wall.
You should — they go on some great trips.
questions.why: 入ろうかと思う→勧める返事が自然。

sets.script: How long did it take you to finish the essay?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: It was about five pages long.
It's due next week.
About three hours, including editing.
I finished it on the bus.
questions.why: How long did it take＝かかった時間。長さ(pages)ではない。

sets.script: Do you want to grab lunch after the lab?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Lunch was served at the party.
I'd love to, but I have a meeting at noon.
The lab has new equipment.
I grabbed it from the shelf.
questions.why: 誘いへの返事。理由を添えて断っている。

sets.script: Wasn't the seminar supposed to be in Room 210?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Room 210 has a projector.
It was moved to the auditorium this morning.
Yes, I'm supposed to go there.
The seminar was really interesting.
questions.why: 否定疑問で場所の確認。変更を伝えるのが自然。

sets.script: I heard the cafeteria is closed for repairs.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: I heard it on the radio, too, about music.
The repairs were cheap.
Then let's try the café in the student center.
Yes, I'm closing the door.
questions.why: 閉まっている→代わりの場所を提案。

sets.script: Who's in charge of booking the room for our study group?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The room is booked every Tuesday.
I'm studying in my room.
We charge five dollars.
Mina said she'd take care of it.
questions.why: Who に人で答える。

sets.script: Can I pay for the field trip by card?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Only cash, I'm afraid.
I'll send you a card.
The trip is to the museum.
Yes, the field is very big.
questions.why: 支払い方法の質問。cash のみと答えている。

sets.script: This assignment is much harder than I expected.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: It was assigned by the professor.
I expected you at three.
Maybe we could work on it together.
Yes, it's very hard to find.
questions.why: 難しいという嘆き→一緒にやろうと提案。

sets.script: When are the results of the exam going to be posted?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The exam was in the main hall.
Probably by the end of next week.
It resulted in a good grade.
I posted the letter this morning.
questions.why: When に時期で答える。post の別の意味に注意。

sets.script: Shouldn't we email the professor about the deadline?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Good idea — I'll write to her now.
I don't have her phone.
The deadline is a long line.
We should leave by email.
questions.why: 提案に賛成して行動を申し出る。

sets.script: I left my umbrella in the lecture hall.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The hall is very large.
It's raining in the lecture.
I left early, too.
The lost and found is next to the main office.
questions.why: 忘れ物→遺失物の場所を教える。

sets.script: Are you going home for the winter break?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Yes, winter is my favorite season.
My home has three bedrooms.
No, I'm staying here to work on my thesis.
The break was only five minutes.
questions.why: 帰省するか→No と理由。

sets.script: The professor wants our drafts by Thursday instead of Friday.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Friday is a holiday next month.
Really? Then I'd better start tonight.
The draft is on the second page.
She drafted it on Thursday.
questions.why: 締め切りが早まった→焦って予定を変える返事。

sets.script: What did you think of the guest speaker?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Her talk was more practical than I expected.
The guest stayed for two nights.
I think it's in the hall.
She's speaking at four.
questions.why: 感想をたずねられている。

sets.script: Is this seat taken?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Yes, I took the bus.
I'll take it to class.
It's a comfortable chair.
No, go ahead.
questions.why: 席が空いているか→No, go ahead が定番。

sets.script: I'm not sure which topic to choose for my paper.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The paper is in the printer.
I'm sure it's on the topic.
Choose the paper size first.
Why don't you ask your advisor for suggestions?
questions.why: 迷っている相手へアドバイス。

sets.script: Did you register for next semester's classes?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Yes, but one of them was already full.
I registered the car.
The register is near the door.
Next semester starts in fall.
questions.why: 登録したか→Yes と状況。register の別の意味に注意。

sets.script: Let's meet in front of the gym at six.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The gym closes on Sundays.
Six people came to the gym.
Sounds good. See you then.
I met him in front of the store.
questions.why: 待ち合わせの提案に同意。

sets.script: How do I get permission to use the chemistry lab on weekends?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: I got permission yesterday, too.
You need to fill out a form at the department office.
Chemistry is fun on weekends.
The lab is on the third floor.
questions.why: How do I …? に手順で答える。

sets.script: Your presentation was really clear.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Thanks — I practiced it a lot.
I presented it on Monday.
Yes, the sky was clear.
It was clearly yours.
questions.why: ほめられたらお礼と一言。

sets.script: Do you know if the bookstore sells used textbooks?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The bookstore is very old.
I know the textbook well.
I used it last semester.
Yes, they have a section in the back.
questions.why: 売っているか→Yes と場所。

sets.script: Hasn't the shuttle bus come yet?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Yes, I've come by bus.
It came from the airport last year.
It's running late because of the snow.
The shuttle has twenty seats.
questions.why: まだ来ないのか→遅れの理由。

sets.script: I'd like to change my advisor. Where should I start?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Start the car in the morning.
Talk to the department secretary first.
My advisor is very kind.
I'd like to change, too.
questions.why: どこから始めるか→最初にすることを答える。

sets.script: Are you taking the advanced writing course next term?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: I'd like to, if it fits my schedule.
No, I took the bus.
I wrote it during the break.
The writing center is downstairs.
questions.why: 来学期とるか→予定に合えば、と答えるのが自然。took / wrote は音や連想のひっかけ。

sets.script: How did your interview for the research job go?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: It goes to the science building.
Better than I expected, I think.
I put it near the window.
The research is about plants.
questions.why: How did … go?＝どうだった？ 結果の感想で答える。

sets.script: Why don't we review the chapter together before the quiz?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: Because I didn't review it.
The quiz had ten questions.
Good idea. How about tomorrow at lunch?
Chapter five is my favorite.
questions.why: Why don't we …? は提案。理由（Because）で答えるのはひっかけ。

sets.script: Didn't you say you'd already paid the club fee?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The club meets on Fridays.
Yes, I'd like to join a club.
The fee is for new members.
I meant to, but I forgot.
questions.why: 払ったと言わなかった？→払うつもりだったが忘れた、が自然な返事。

sets.script: Which of these two topics do you think is easier to research?

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: The second one has more sources.
I researched it for two hours.
Yes, it was easy.
Both of them went to the library.
questions.why: Which …? に Yes では答えない。どちらかを理由と一緒に選ぶ。

sets.script: I'm worried I won't finish my project in time.

questions.q: Choose the best response.
choices: It's about time to go.
Maybe you could ask for an extension.
I finished it at nine.
The project room is upstairs.
questions.why: 心配ごとへの返事→提案（期限の延長を頼む）。time / finish は語のひっかけ。

parts.title: Listening: Listen to a Conversation
parts.desc: キャンパスでの2人の短い会話を聞いて2問
parts.tip: 最初のやりとりで「誰が何に困っているか」をつかむ。後半の提案や決めたこと（I'll … / Why don't you …）が次の行動の問いになる。
parts.intro: Listen to a conversation. Then answer the questions.

sets.script: Today let's look at an animal that lives in two very different worlds: the frog. Most frogs begin life as eggs laid in water. The eggs hatch into tadpoles, which breathe through gills and swim with a tail, a lot like fish. Over a few weeks or months, the tadpole goes through a dramatic change called metamorphosis. It grows legs, its tail is absorbed into its body, and it develops lungs so it can breathe air. Now, here's something interesting. Adult frogs also breathe through their skin. That's why their skin has to stay moist. And it's also why frogs are often called indicator species. Because chemicals in the water and air pass easily through their skin, frogs are very sensitive to pollution. So when frog populations in an area start to decline, scientists take it as an early warning that something may be wrong with the environment.

sets.script: Last week we talked about how minerals form. Today I want to focus on one way geologists identify them: hardness. In the early nineteenth century, a scale was developed that ranks minerals from one to ten. Talc, which is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, is a one. Diamond, the hardest natural mineral, is a ten. The test is simple. If mineral A can scratch mineral B, then A is harder. Now, one common misunderstanding is that the scale is evenly spaced. It isn't. The scale only tells you the order. Diamond, at ten, is actually several times harder than corundum, at nine. So the jump from nine to ten is much bigger than the jump from one to two. In the field, geologists often carry simple tools to test hardness — a steel nail, a piece of glass, even a copper coin — because these have known positions on the scale.

sets.script: When we think of the Silk Road, we often picture a single road running from China to the Mediterranean. In reality, it was a huge network of routes over land and sea, and very few traders ever traveled the whole distance. Instead, goods were passed from one merchant to the next, often changing hands many times. A bolt of silk might be traded at a market in Central Asia, carried further west by another group, and sold again before reaching its final buyer. Each time, the price went up. And it wasn't just silk. Spices, paper, glass, horses, and precious metals moved along these routes. But perhaps the most important things that traveled weren't goods at all. Ideas did too: religions, languages, farming techniques, and even mathematical knowledge. In that sense, the Silk Road was as much a network of communication as a network of trade.

sets.script: Let's talk about why some colors seem to move or vibrate in a painting, even though the paint is perfectly still. It has to do with something called complementary colors. On a color wheel, complementary colors sit directly opposite each other — red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. When you place two complementary colors side by side, each one makes the other look more intense. Painters have used this for centuries, but in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries some artists made it a central part of their work. By putting small dots or strokes of complementary colors next to each other, they created surfaces that seemed to shimmer. There's actually a biological reason for this. When you stare at one color for a while, the cells in your eye that respond to it get tired, and you start to see its complement. Artists didn't always know the science, but they understood the effect from experience.

questions.q: What does the professor imply about the artists?

sets.script: Have you ever noticed that you remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones? This idea goes back to early research in psychology. A researcher noticed that waiters could remember complex orders perfectly — until the bill was paid. After that, they forgot the details almost immediately. To test this, experiments were designed in which people were given a series of simple tasks, like puzzles, and were interrupted before finishing some of them. Later, when asked to recall the tasks, participants remembered the interrupted ones about twice as often. This became known as the Zeigarnik effect, after the researcher. Now, later studies have shown that the effect isn't always strong; it depends on things like how motivated people are to finish. But it does suggest a practical study tip. If you stop studying in the middle of a section rather than at the end, you may find it easier to pick up where you left off.

questions.q: What observation led to the early research?
choices: People could not finish simple tasks.
Waiters forgot orders once the customers had paid.
Students remembered puzzles better than words.
Customers often forgot what they ordered.
questions.why: waiters … remember orders perfectly — until the bill was paid。

questions.q: What did the experiments find?
choices: Interrupted tasks were remembered more often.
Finished tasks were remembered twice as often.
Interruptions made people angry.
Puzzles were harder than other tasks.
questions.why: remembered the interrupted ones about twice as often。

questions.q: What does the professor say about later studies?
choices: They showed the effect is stronger in waiters.
They proved the effect does not exist.
They used only puzzles.
They found the effect depends on factors such as motivation.
questions.why: isn't always strong; it depends on … how motivated people are。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention stopping in the middle of a section?
choices: To criticize students who study too long
To show that interruptions are harmful
To give a practical application of the effect
To explain how the experiments were designed
questions.why: it does suggest a practical study tip。

sets.script: Today's topic is something economists call the tragedy of the commons. Imagine a village pasture that anyone can use to feed their cows. For each farmer, adding one more cow is a good deal: the farmer gets all the benefit of the extra milk, while the cost — a little less grass — is shared by everyone. The problem is that every farmer thinks the same way. So more and more cows are added until the grass is gone, and everyone loses. The same pattern appears with fishing in open waters, with groundwater, and even with traffic on a free road. Now, for a long time, people assumed the only solutions were government rules or private ownership. But research on real communities found a third option. Many groups have managed shared resources successfully for generations by setting their own rules — limiting how much each member can take and watching each other to make sure the rules are followed.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the tragedy of the commons?
choices: Milk prices rise when grass is scarce.
Governments always manage land poorly.
Individuals acting in their own interest can destroy a shared resource.
Villages should not allow farmers to own cows.
questions.why: 各自が得をしようとして、全員が損をする。

questions.q: Why does each farmer want to add another cow?
choices: The farmer gains the full benefit but shares the cost.
Cows eat less grass in large groups.
The pasture is owned by the farmer.
The government pays for each cow.
questions.why: gets all the benefit … the cost is shared by everyone。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention fishing and traffic?
choices: To explain how roads are built
To argue that fishing should be banned
To compare different types of farming
To show that the same problem occurs in other situations
questions.why: The same pattern appears with fishing … traffic。

questions.q: What third option does the professor describe?
choices: Selling the pasture to one farmer
Communities creating and enforcing their own rules
Removing all cows from the pasture
Asking a government to set prices
questions.why: groups … setting their own rules … watching each other。

sets.script: Most people think of deserts as places where nothing grows. But many plants have adapted to survive there. Let's look at three strategies. First, some plants store water. Cactuses, for example, have thick stems that can swell after rain and shrink during long dry periods. Second, some plants reduce water loss. Instead of broad leaves, cactuses have spines, which lose much less water and also protect the plant from animals. Many desert plants also open the tiny holes in their surfaces, called stomata, only at night, when it's cooler and less water evaporates. The third strategy is avoidance. Some desert flowers spend most of their lives as seeds in the soil. When a heavy rain finally comes, they sprout, flower, and produce new seeds within just a few weeks, and then they die. So the desert can suddenly fill with color for a short time after a storm.

questions.q: How does the professor organize the talk?
choices: By describing three survival strategies
By comparing deserts on different continents
By listing plants from smallest to largest
By telling the history of desert research
questions.why: Let's look at three strategies。

questions.q: What is one function of cactus spines mentioned in the talk?
choices: They help the plant grow taller.
They collect rainwater.
They protect the plant from animals.
They attract insects.
questions.why: lose much less water and also protect the plant from animals。

questions.q: Why do many desert plants open their stomata only at night?
choices: They need moonlight to grow.
Animals are less active at night.
The soil is wetter at night.
Less water is lost when it is cooler.
questions.why: when it's cooler and less water evaporates。

questions.q: What can be inferred about the desert flowers described at the end?
choices: They live for many years above ground.
They complete their life cycle very quickly after rain.
They grow only in winter.
They store water in thick stems.
questions.why: 数週間で発芽・開花・種まで終えて枯れる。

sets.script: In the early days of photography, many painters worried that the camera would make them unnecessary. After all, a photograph could record a face or a landscape more accurately than any brush. And in fact, the market for small painted portraits did shrink as photography studios opened. But the effect on art turned out to be more complicated. Freed from the job of simply copying what they saw, some painters began to explore what a camera couldn't do — expressing emotion, playing with color, or showing a scene from several angles at once. At the same time, photography itself influenced painting. Photographs captured moments that the eye usually misses, such as the exact position of a running horse's legs. Some painters studied these images closely and changed the way they showed motion. So rather than replacing painting, photography pushed it in new directions.

questions.q: What did many painters fear when photography appeared?
choices: That photography would be too expensive
That photographs would damage paintings
That studios would stop selling paint
That cameras would replace their work
questions.why: the camera would make them unnecessary。

questions.q: What does the professor say about small painted portraits?
choices: They became more popular.
There was less demand for them.
They were painted only by photographers.
They were copied from photographs.
questions.why: the market for small painted portraits did shrink。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a running horse?
choices: To explain why painters disliked photography
To describe a famous painting
To illustrate how photographs revealed details people normally miss
To show that horses were difficult to photograph
questions.why: moments that the eye usually misses の例。

questions.q: What is the professor's main conclusion?
choices: Photography encouraged painting to change and develop.
Photography completely replaced painting.
Painters should avoid using photographs.
Painting had no effect on photography.
questions.why: rather than replacing painting, photography pushed it in new directions。

sets.script: Why do bubbles form in markets? A bubble happens when the price of something — houses, stocks, even flowers — rises far above what most experts think it's really worth. One key factor is expectations. If people believe a price will keep rising, they buy, not because they need the item, but because they expect to sell it later for more. That buying pushes the price higher, which seems to confirm their belief, and even more people join in. For a while, this cycle feeds itself. But at some point, buyers start to doubt that prices can go any higher. When enough people try to sell at the same time, prices can fall very quickly. Economists still debate how to identify a bubble before it bursts. The difficulty is that a rising price doesn't always mean a bubble; sometimes the value has genuinely increased.

questions.q: How does the professor define a bubble?
choices: A price far above what most experts believe something is worth
Any price that rises quickly
A sudden fall in the price of flowers
A market where nothing is sold
questions.why: rises far above what most experts think it's really worth。

questions.q: According to the professor, why do people buy during a bubble?
choices: They need the item for daily use.
Prices are lower than usual.
They expect to sell later at a higher price.
The government encourages them.
questions.why: because they expect to sell it later for more。

questions.q: What causes prices to fall quickly?
choices: New buyers entering the market
A shortage of the item
Experts changing their definitions
Many people trying to sell at once
questions.why: When enough people try to sell at the same time。

questions.q: Why is it difficult to identify a bubble in advance?
choices: Bubbles happen only with houses.
A rising price may reflect a real increase in value.
Prices never rise for long.
Economists do not study prices.
questions.why: a rising price doesn't always mean a bubble。

sets.script: Today I want to talk about hibernation. Many people think hibernating animals are simply sleeping through the winter. That's not quite right. Hibernation is a state in which an animal lowers its body temperature, heart rate, and breathing to save energy when food is scarce. A ground squirrel's heart, for example, can slow from about two hundred beats a minute to fewer than ten. Now, here's the surprising part. Every week or two, most hibernators warm back up to their normal temperature for a few hours, then cool down again. These warm periods use up much of the animal's stored fat. So why do it? One idea is that the body needs to repair itself, which it can't do properly when it's cold. Interestingly, during these warm periods, many animals fall into ordinary sleep. So, in a strange way, they may need to wake from hibernation in order to sleep.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: What hibernation is and why hibernating animals regularly warm up
Why ground squirrels need more food in winter
How animals find safe places to spend the winter
Why sleep is less important than hibernation
questions.why: 冬眠の定義→定期的に体を温める謎→その理由の説。

questions.q: Why does the professor mention a ground squirrel's heart rate?
choices: To compare squirrels with larger animals
To show how much an animal's body slows during hibernation
To explain why squirrels store fat
To show that squirrels do not truly hibernate
questions.why: 200回から10回未満へ＝体の働きがどれだけ落ちるかの例。

questions.q: According to the professor, what is a cost of the warm periods?
choices: They make the heart beat irregularly.
They wake up other animals nearby.
They use up much of the animal's stored fat.
They stop the body from repairing itself.
questions.why: These warm periods use up much of the animal's stored fat。

questions.q: What does the professor imply at the end of the talk?
choices: Animals sleep more deeply during hibernation.
Hibernation and sleep are the same thing.
Animals do not need sleep in winter.
Hibernation may not give animals the benefits of normal sleep.
questions.why: 眠るために冬眠から目覚める＝冬眠は普通の睡眠の代わりにならない。

sets.script: Today we're going to look at how words change their meanings over time. One common pattern is broadening, where a meaning becomes more general. Bird, for instance, once meant only a young bird; now it means any bird. The opposite pattern is narrowing. In older English, meat meant food of any kind, but today it refers only to the flesh of animals. A third pattern is that a word can become more positive or more negative. Nice is a famous example. Hundreds of years ago, it meant foolish. Its meaning shifted several times before it became the pleasant word we use today. Why do these changes happen? Often, speakers start using a word in new situations, and over generations, the new use simply becomes normal. A dictionary, then, is really just a snapshot of a language that never stops moving.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
choices: Patterns in how the meanings of words change over time
How dictionaries are written
Why English has borrowed many words
How children learn new words
questions.why: 語の意味の変化の3つの型と、その理由。

questions.q: Which word does the professor give as an example of narrowing?
choices: Bird
Meat
Nice

questions.why: meat は食べ物全般→動物の肉だけ＝意味が狭くなった。bird は広くなった例。

questions.q: What does the professor say about the word nice?
choices: It has always meant pleasant.
It used to refer to food.
Its meaning changed several times and became positive.
It is an example of broadening.
questions.why: 昔は foolish の意味。何度か変わって今のよい意味に。

questions.q: According to the professor, why do word meanings change?
choices: Dictionaries change the definitions.
Teachers correct the old uses.
Words become shorter over time.
People use words in new situations, and the new uses become normal.
questions.why: speakers start using a word in new situations … the new use simply becomes normal。

parts.title: Writing: Write an Email
parts.desc: 状況に合わせてメールを書く（7分）
parts.tip: 書き出し（Dear …,）→用件1文→指示された3つの点→結び（Thank you … / Best regards,）。3つの点を全部入れることが一番大事。相手に合わせて丁寧さを変える。
parts.intro: Read the situation and write an email. You have 7 minutes.

sets.prompt:
You are taking an online course in environmental science. The professor has asked each student to visit a local park and write a short report, but the park near you has been closed for repairs for the next month.

Write an email to your professor. In your email:
- explain the problem
- suggest another way to complete the assignment
- ask whether the deadline can be changed
sets.note: 3つの点をすべて書く。丁寧な書き出しと結びを入れる。

sets.prompt:
You recently joined a university hiking club. The club's next trip is on a weekend when you have a family event, but you would still like to take part in the club's activities.

Write an email to the club leader. In your email:
- explain why you cannot go on the next trip
- describe what kind of activities you enjoy
- ask how else you can be involved this month
sets.note: 理由・好み・質問の3つを段落かつなぎ語で分ける。

sets.prompt:
You bought a used textbook from the campus bookstore. When you got home, you found that several pages were missing.

Write an email to the bookstore manager. In your email:
- describe the problem with the book
- explain why you need the book soon
- say what you would like the store to do
sets.note: 苦情でも丁寧に。具体的に（何ページ・いつ必要か）。

sets.prompt:
Your study group has been meeting in a library room every Tuesday evening. This week, the library has told you the room is no longer available on Tuesdays.

Write an email to the members of your study group. In your email:
- explain what has happened
- suggest a new time or place
- ask members to reply with their preference
sets.note: 仲間あてなので少しくだけてよいが、文は正確に。

sets.prompt:
You would like to work as a research assistant for a professor whose class you enjoyed last semester. You have not talked with the professor about this before.

Write an email to the professor. In your email:
- introduce yourself and mention the class you took
- explain why you are interested in the research
- ask whether any positions are available
sets.note: 自己紹介→理由→質問の順。I am writing to … で始めると楽。

sets.prompt:
The air conditioner in your dormitory room has stopped working, and it has been very hot for several days. You reported it once, but nobody has come to fix it.

Write an email to the housing office. In your email:
- describe the problem and how long it has lasted
- explain how it is affecting you
- request a specific action
sets.note: 経過（いつ報告したか）を入れると説得力が出る。

sets.prompt:
A classmate lent you a book for a project, but you accidentally spilled coffee on it and damaged several pages.

Write an email to your classmate. In your email:
- explain what happened
- apologize
- offer a way to make up for the damage
sets.note: 謝罪は具体的に。償いの方法を1つ提案する。

sets.prompt:
You read on the university website that the campus gym is planning to reduce its weekend hours. You use the gym mostly on weekends.

Write an email to the gym director. In your email:
- explain how you use the gym
- describe how the change would affect you and other students
- suggest an alternative
sets.note: 反対意見＋代案。感情ではなく理由で。

sets.prompt:
You are organizing an extra study session for students in your statistics course before the midterm exam. You would like to use a classroom in the mathematics building.

Write an email to the department office. In your email:
- explain why you want to use a room
- give the number of students and the time you need it
- ask whether a projector is available
sets.note: 用件→人数と時間→備品の質問。数字は具体的に。

sets.prompt:
You missed a required lab session this week because you had a doctor's appointment that you could not change.

Write an email to the teaching assistant for the course. In your email:
- explain why you missed the lab
- ask how you can make up the work
- ask whether you need any materials before then
sets.note: 謝る→理由→2つの質問。質問は Could you …? などで丁寧に。

sets.prompt:
For the past two weeks, a student who lives next to you in the dormitory has been playing loud music late at night. You have already asked them once to turn it down.

Write an email to the residence hall advisor. In your email:
- describe the problem
- explain how it is affecting you
- suggest a solution
sets.note: 相手を責めすぎず、事実→影響→解決案。already asked once も入れる。

sets.prompt:
A café near campus has posted an advertisement for part-time staff. You are interested in the job.

Write an email to the café manager. In your email:
- introduce yourself
- describe experience or skills that make you a good fit
- ask about the working hours
sets.note: 自己紹介→経験・強み→勤務時間の質問。応募の気持ちを最初に。

sets.prompt:
You borrowed a book from the university library, but you cannot find it anywhere, and it is due in three days.

Write an email to the librarian. In your email:
- explain what happened

sets.prompt:
You are applying for a summer program in science, and you need a letter of recommendation. Your former high school science teacher knows your work well.

Write an email to your former teacher. In your email:
- describe the program you are applying for

- tell the teacher the deadline and how to send the letter

sets.prompt:
You recently attended a free workshop on public speaking organized by the student center, and you found it very helpful.

Write an email to the workshop organizer. In your email:
- thank the organizer
- explain which part of the workshop was most useful and why
- suggest a topic for a future workshop

sets.prompt:
A friend from another country is visiting your city next month and has asked you for advice about the trip.

Write an email to your friend. In your email:
- recommend two places to visit
- explain the best way to get around the city
- suggest a day when you can meet
sets.note: 友だちあてなので Hi … ! でよい。おすすめ2つ→交通→会う日。

parts.title: Writing: Write for an Academic Discussion
parts.desc: 教授の問いと学生2人の投稿を読み、自分の意見を書く（10分・100語以上）
parts.tip: 1文目で自分の立場をはっきり書く。他の学生の意見に一言触れ、2人が言っていない理由か具体例を足す。最後に短くまとめる。
parts.intro: Read the professor's question and the two student posts. Write a post that adds your own opinion to the discussion. You have 10 minutes.

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on psychology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Many students study while listening to music. Some researchers say music helps people stay focused, while others say it divides attention. In your experience, does listening to music while studying help or hurt learning? Why?

Maya: Music helps me a lot. When I study in silence, I get bored and start checking my phone. Calm music without words keeps me at my desk longer.

Tom: I think it depends on the task. Music is fine for simple work like organizing notes, but when I read difficult material, any sound distracts me.
sets.note: 自分の立場を最初に。2人の意見に一言触れ、新しい理由か例を足す。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some cities charge drivers a fee to enter the city center during busy hours. Supporters say it reduces traffic and pollution; critics say it is unfair to people with lower incomes. Do you think such fees are a good policy? Why or why not?

Lena: I support the fees. Traffic in city centers wastes time and damages health. If driving costs more, people will choose buses and trains.

Omar: I disagree. Workers who live far away may have no good public transport. A fee would punish people who have no choice.
sets.note: Lena と Omar のどちらに近いかを示し、2人が言っていない理由を1つ。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on history. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: When we study history, we can focus on famous leaders and major events, or on the daily lives of ordinary people. Which approach do you think helps students understand the past better? Why?

Kenji: Leaders and major events shaped everything else. Without understanding them, the daily lives of ordinary people do not make sense.

Sara: I prefer learning about ordinary people. Most people in history were farmers and workers, and their lives tell us what the past was really like.
sets.note: どちらか一方を選ぶか、両方の良さを言ってから自分の重みづけを示す。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on biology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Zoos spend large amounts of money to protect endangered animals through breeding programs. Some people believe that money would be better spent protecting the animals' natural habitats. Which do you think is more important, and why?

Ana: Protecting habitats is more important. If the forests and wetlands disappear, there will be nowhere to return the animals bred in zoos.

David: Zoos are necessary because some species are so rare that they could disappear before their habitats are protected. Breeding programs buy time.
sets.note: 具体例（森・海など）を1つ入れると展開点が上がる。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some universities now require all students to take at least one course outside their major, such as an art course for engineering students. Do you think this kind of requirement is valuable? Why or why not?

Chris: Yes. Taking a course in a different field helps students think creatively and solve problems in new ways.

Yuna: I am not sure. University is expensive, and students should be free to spend their time on courses that prepare them for their careers.
sets.note: 自分の経験を短く1つ入れると説得力が出る。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on art. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Many museums now offer virtual tours online, where people can view artworks from home. Do you think virtual tours can replace visiting a museum in person? Why or why not?

Liam: Virtual tours are great because anyone can see famous works without traveling. For many people, this is the only way to see them.

Nora: Seeing a painting online is not the same. The size, texture, and atmosphere of a real museum cannot be shown on a screen.
sets.note: 「完全には置き換えられない、ただし…」のような条件付きの立場もよい。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: More companies are allowing employees to work from home several days a week. Some say this improves workers' lives; others worry that it weakens teamwork. In your opinion, what is the biggest effect of working from home, and why?

Paulo: The biggest effect is more free time. Without a long commute, people can exercise, cook, and spend time with family.

Hana: I think the biggest effect is on young employees. They miss the chance to learn by watching experienced colleagues in the office.
sets.note: 「一番大きい影響」を1つに絞り、理由と例で支える。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on environmental science. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: To reduce plastic waste, governments can either ban certain plastic products or encourage companies to develop better recycling systems. Which approach do you think is more effective? Why?

Isabel: Bans are more effective. Recycling has existed for decades, yet most plastic still ends up in landfills or the ocean.

Marcus: Bans can create new problems, such as replacing plastic with materials that use more energy. Improving recycling solves the problem without these side effects.
sets.note: どちらかを選び、相手の意見への反論を1文入れると構成がよくなる。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on business. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Many companies now allow employees to work from home several days a week. Some managers believe this makes workers more productive, while others worry that it weakens teamwork. Do you think companies should continue to allow working from home? Why or why not?

Aisha: Yes, they should. Without a long commute, people have more energy and time. In my part-time job, I finish my reports faster at home because there are fewer interruptions.

Ben: I think a few days at home is fine, but not too many. New employees especially need to be in the office to learn from experienced coworkers by watching and asking questions.
sets.note: 立場→2人に一言→新しい理由（費用・地域・健康など）か具体例。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on computer science. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some universities now require all students, whatever their major, to take at least one course in computer programming. Supporters say coding is a basic skill today; critics say students should be free to choose their own courses. Should programming be required for all students? Why or why not?

Carlos: I support the requirement. Almost every job uses software now, and even a basic course teaches you how to solve problems step by step.

Mei: I disagree. Students already have many required courses. A course in statistics or writing might be more useful for someone studying history or art.
sets.note: 賛成か反対かを最初に。Carlos か Mei の理由に足す形で、自分の経験を1つ。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some cities have turned busy streets in their downtown areas into pedestrian zones where cars are not allowed. Do you think this is a good idea for cities? Why or why not?

Elif: It's a great idea. When cars are removed, streets become quieter and safer, and more people walk around and visit local shops.

Jonah: It can hurt some people. Delivery trucks and older residents who cannot walk far depend on being able to drive close to stores.
sets.note: どちらかを選び、2人が言っていない点（空気・観光・バスとの組み合わせ等）を足す。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on public health. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some schools have removed sugary drinks from their vending machines to improve students' health. Others argue that students should learn to make their own choices. Which approach do you think is better? Why?

Farah: Removing the drinks is better. Young people are strongly influenced by what is easy to buy, and many don't think about the long-term effects of sugar.

Victor: Banning things rarely works. Students just buy the drinks at a store nearby. Teaching them about nutrition would have a longer-lasting effect.
sets.note: 片方に賛成し、もう一方の意見に短く反論すると流れがよい。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on media studies. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Many people now get most of their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. In your opinion, is this change mostly positive or mostly negative? Why?

Grace: Mostly positive. Social media lets people hear about events immediately and from many different voices, not just from a few large news organizations.

Ibrahim: I see it as negative. Posts are often shared before anyone checks whether they are true, and people tend to see only opinions they already agree with.
sets.note: 立場→理由→具体例（自分や家族の使い方）。最後に一文でまとめる。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on anthropology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: When people move to a new country, some try to adopt the customs of their new home quickly, while others work hard to keep the traditions of their original culture. Which do you think is more important for newcomers? Why?

Hugo: Adapting quickly matters most. Learning local customs helps newcomers find jobs and make friends, which makes life in a new place much easier.

Tara: Keeping your own traditions is just as important. They give people a sense of identity and help families stay connected across generations.
sets.note: どちらか、または両立の立場でもよい。ただし理由ははっきり。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on linguistics. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: Some people believe that children should begin learning a foreign language in their first year of elementary school. Others think it is better to wait until students are older and have a strong foundation in their first language. Which view do you agree with? Why?

Irene: Starting early is better. Young children copy sounds easily and are not afraid of making mistakes, so they often develop better pronunciation.

Kofi: I think it's better to wait. If children start too young, they may get confused, and schools may not have enough qualified teachers for young learners.
sets.note: どちらかを選び、自分の学習経験を例にすると説得力が出る。

sets.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on engineering. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

Professor: When cities need new infrastructure, they can either build large, expensive projects such as new highways, or spend the same money repairing and improving existing roads and bridges. Which approach do you think is wiser? Why?

Jamal: Repairing what we already have is wiser. Many roads and bridges are old, and fixing them first prevents larger costs later.

Sofia: New projects are sometimes necessary. If a city is growing quickly, old roads simply cannot handle the traffic, no matter how well they are repaired.
sets.note: どちらかを選び、相手側の理由に「確かに〜だが」と一言触れる。
